questions.q: What does AVG() fail to tell you that VAR()/STDEV() capture?
options: How spread out the values are around the mean
The total sum of all values
Whether any value is NULL
The number of rows in the table
questions.explain: Two sets of numbers can share the same average while having very different spreads — variance and standard deviation measure that spread.

options: The square root of variance
The square of variance
The same thing as the average
The difference between the max and min values
questions.explain: STDEV() = square root of VAR() — this is exactly why it's easier to interpret.

questions.q: Why is STDEV() more commonly reported in practice than raw VAR()?
options: STDEV brings the units back to the original scale (e.g. dollars), while VAR is in squared units that are hard to interpret directly
VAR() is deprecated in SQL Server
STDEV() is always a smaller, more 'convenient' number
VAR() cannot be combined with GROUP BY
questions.explain: A variance of 22,500 (dollars-squared) is much harder to reason about than a standard deviation of $150.

questions.q: Do VAR() and STDEV() behave structurally like other aggregate functions covered in this chapter?
options: Yes — they skip NULL, work with GROUP BY, and can be filtered with HAVING, same as COUNT/SUM/AVG
No, they require entirely different syntax
They cannot be used with GROUP BY under any circumstances
They are the only aggregate functions that include NULL as zero
questions.explain: There's nothing structurally new here — same aggregate function rules apply as SUM, AVG, MIN, and MAX.

questions.q: When would you specifically reach for VAR/STDEV instead of just AVG?
options: When the spread/consistency of the data matters as much as its center, e.g. flagging wildly inconsistent pricing
Whenever working with text columns instead of numbers
Only when GROUP BY is not being used
VAR/STDEV should always replace AVG entirely
questions.explain: AVG alone can hide wide variability — STDEV surfaces it, useful for identifying volatility or inconsistency.
